lead: A radar receiver never sees a clean echo; it sees echo plus noise. Detection is the decision: target present or absent, from one noisy observation. The matched filter is the receiver that gives the largest possible peak signal-to-noise ratio for a known pulse shape. A constant false alarm rate (CFAR) threshold then keeps false alarms steady when clutter changes. This chain is used in airport surveillance, weather radars and missile seekers.
prereq: You need: echo power and minimum detectable signal from 6.2, and noise figure and bandwidth from Unit 5, Noise figure, cascaded noise and sensitivity.

sections.h3: The detection problem and matched filter

blocks.text: Detection is a two-choice problem. Under H0 the input is r(t)=n(t). Under H1 it is r(t)=s(t)+n(t). Here s(t) is the known received pulse in volts; n(t) is white Gaussian noise with two-sided power spectral density N0/2 in W/Hz. N0 is the one-sided noise density in W/Hz. The receiver must decide H1 or H0 from one observation of length T.

Pass r(t) through a linear filter h(t) and sample at time T. The peak signal-to-noise ratio is the signal power at T divided by the noise power at T. The filter that maximises this ratio is the matched filter.

blocks.where: h(t) is the filter impulse response; s(T − t) is the received pulse reversed in time and shifted to end at the sampling instant T.
SNRmax is the peak power signal-to-noise ratio at the filter output; E is the pulse energy in joules, E = ∫ s²(t) dt over the pulse; N0 is the one-sided noise power spectral density in W/Hz.

blocks.text: The pulse shape cancels out. Only the energy E matters, not whether the pulse is rectangular, triangular or Gaussian. A correlation receiver multiplies r(t) by s(t), integrates over T and samples at T. It gives the same number, so matched filtering and correlation are two views of one operation.
For a rectangular pulse of average power Pt in watts and width τ in seconds, E=Ptτ. Then SNRmax=2Ptτ/N0. The matched filter is an integrate-and-dump over τ seconds.

After the filter, the detector decides. An envelope detector gives |y(T)|. A square-law detector gives |y(T)|². Noise alone gives a Rayleigh-distributed envelope. For envelope voltage V and threshold VT, Pfa=exp(−VT²/(2σ²)). Pfa is the probability of false alarm; σ² is the variance of each quadrature noise component in V².

Raising VT lowers Pfa but also lowers Pd, the probability of detecting a real target. The Neyman–Pearson rule fixes Pfa first and then chooses the threshold that gives the largest Pd. Plotting Pd against Pfa gives the receiver operating characteristic, or ROC. Signal plus noise has a Rician envelope, and Pd comes from the Rician or Marcum Q function.

Coherent integration adds complex matched-filter outputs from N pulses before detection. For equal pulses the SNR rises about N times. Noncoherent integration adds envelope outputs after detection. It is simpler but loses some SNR. Swerling models (Swerling 1 to 4) only name how target cross section fluctuates; they change the ROC, not the matched filter.

A fixed threshold fails when clutter or receiver noise changes. A strong rain cell raises the noise mean, so the same VT gives a high Pfa. CFAR estimates the local noise from neighbouring range cells. In cell-averaging CFAR, the cell under test (CUT) is the cell being tested. Guard cells on each side are left out so target spill-over does not bias the estimate. Training cells further out are averaged to give noise estimate Z.

blocks.where: Pfa is the required false-alarm probability; α is the threshold multiplier, so the threshold is αZ; N is the number of training cells used in the average Z.

blocks.text: Solve this for α when Pfa is specified. The estimate Z is noisy, so CFAR needs extra SNR compared with a known fixed threshold. That extra SNR is CFAR loss. Ordered-statistic and greatest-of CFAR are common variants.

Waveform design adds resolution without shortening the pulse. A linear FM chirp sweeps frequency by B Hz over τ seconds. The matched filter compresses it to a pulse of width about 1/B seconds. The time-bandwidth product τB is the compression ratio. Range resolution is ΔR=c/(2B); c is the speed of light, 3×10⁸ m/s, and B is the chirp bandwidth in Hz. Long τ gives energy for detection range; large B gives fine range resolution.

figure.caption: The chain turns a noisy IF echo into a target decision. The threshold block sets its level from neighbouring range cells, so a change in clutter does not change the false-alarm rate.

spec.title: Detection chain
spec.aria: Detection chain: the noisy echo passes through the matched filter, is envelope detected, and its level is compared with a threshold that is set from the average of neighbouring range cells.

examples.question: A radar echo at the receiver input has Pr = 1×10⁻¹³ W. The pulse width is τ = 1 μs. The receiver has noise bandwidth B = 1 MHz, noise figure F = 10 dB (a ratio of 10), at T0 = 290 K. Find the input SNR and the matched-filter output SNR. Use k = 1.38×10⁻²³ J/K.
steps: Convert the noise figure to a ratio: F = 10 dB gives F = 10.
Find the receiver noise power: N = k T0 F B = 1.38×10⁻²³ × 290 × 10 × 1×10⁶ = 4.002×10⁻¹⁴ W ≈ 4.0×10⁻¹⁴ W.
Input SNR = Pr / N = 1×10⁻¹³ / 4.002×10⁻¹⁴ = 2.499 ≈ 2.5. In decibels, 10 log₁₀(2.5) = 3.98 dB ≈ 4.0 dB.
Find the one-sided noise density: N0 = k T0 F = 1.38×10⁻²³ × 290 × 10 = 4.002×10⁻²⁰ W/Hz ≈ 4.0×10⁻²⁰ W/Hz.
Find the pulse energy: E = Pr τ = 1×10⁻¹³ × 1×10⁻⁶ = 1.0×10⁻¹⁹ J.
Matched-filter output SNR = 2E / N0 = 2×1.0×10⁻¹⁹ / 4.002×10⁻²⁰ = 4.998 ≈ 5.0. In decibels, 10 log₁₀(5.0) = 6.99 dB ≈ 7.0 dB.
The gain over the input SNR is 5.0 / 2.5 = 2, that is 3 dB. The matched filter buys a factor of 2 over filtering with bandwidth 1/τ.
examples.answer: The receiver noise is 4.0×10⁻¹⁴ W, input SNR is 2.5 (4.0 dB), N0 is 4.0×10⁻²⁰ W/Hz, pulse energy is 1.0×10⁻¹⁹ J, and matched-filter output SNR is 5.0 (7.0 dB).
examples.check:
import math
k=1.38e-23
T0=290
F=10
B=1e6
Pr=1e-13
tau=1e-6
N=k*T0*F*B
snr_in=Pr/N
snr_in_db=10*math.log10(snr_in)
N0=k*T0*F
E=Pr*tau
snr_out=2*E/N0
snr_out_db=10*math.log10(snr_out)
print(f'{N:.1e}')
print(f'{snr_in:.1f}')
print(f'{snr_in_db:.1f}')
print(f'{N0:.1e}')
print(f'{E:.1e}')
print(f'{snr_out:.1f}')
print(f'{snr_out_db:.1f}')

traps: The matched filter maximises peak SNR, not Pd directly. Pd follows only after the threshold is set by Pfa, and CFAR loss is counted.
Do not mix N0 and N0/2. Use the one-sided N0 in 2E/N0, and note that the two-sided density is N0/2.
Input SNR uses receiver noise bandwidth B. Matched-filter output SNR uses pulse energy E and N0; do not plug B into 2E/N0.
The CFAR multiplier α is not an SNR. It is the factor that multiplies the local noise estimate to set the threshold.
Pulse compression improves range resolution through bandwidth B. It does not create extra pulse energy; energy still comes from pulse width τ.

quiz.q: What is the impulse response of the matched filter for a pulse s(t) sampled at time T?
quiz.a: h(t)=s(T−t), the mirror of the pulse about T.

quiz.q: Why does the pulse shape not change the peak matched-filter SNR?
quiz.a: The peak output SNR is 2E/N0, and the shape affects only how energy is spread in time; only E and N0 set the peak ratio.

quiz.q: A rectangular pulse has Pt=2×10⁻¹³ W, τ=0.5 μs, and N0=4×10⁻²⁰ W/Hz. Find the matched-filter output SNR.
Why does a fixed threshold fail when clutter level rises?
quiz.a: Rising clutter raises the noise mean, so the same threshold gives a higher Pfa. CFAR estimates the local mean and moves the threshold.

quiz.q: For cell-averaging CFAR with N=16 training cells and Pfa=1×10⁻⁴, find α.
Compare coherent and noncoherent integration of N pulses.
quiz.a: Coherent integration adds complex amplitudes before detection and raises SNR about N times. Noncoherent integration adds envelopes after detection; it is simpler but loses SNR.

quiz.q: Write the range resolution of a linear FM chirp radar with bandwidth B.
quiz.a: ΔR=c/(2B), where c is the speed of light and B is the chirp bandwidth.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern radars do the matched filter digitally, often as fast convolution, and use CFAR variants such as ordered-statistic or greatest-of CFAR in real time. Phased-array and MIMO radars add space-time adaptive processing, where the same detection logic runs across antenna elements and pulses. Pulse compression with nonlinear FM or phase codes trades sidelobes against Doppler tolerance. Researchers study knowledge-aided CFAR and learning-based detectors for dense clutter. Search next for CA-CFAR threshold multiplier, Marcum Q function, LFM pulse compression and STAP radar detection.
